text: Ὁ προερχόμενος. Quod tanta ejus vocis λόγος Græcis amplitudo est ac ὁμωνυμία, scite Maximus de illo distinxit, qui ore profertur. Nam λόγος ἐνδιάθετος, mentis sermo ac cordis, illique insitus, de quo tanta in procœmio Scholiorum ad Quæst. ad Thalass. ipse potius actionis parens, præhabensque quidquid in ea bonitatis exsistit. Qua de re ad orat. Gregorii in magnum Athanasium.
anchorLine: χόμενος (a).
en: "The one who proceeds." Because for the Greeks the word logos has so wide a range and is a homonym, Maximus rightly distinguished it from the logos that is uttered by the mouth. For the inward logos (logos endiathetos), the speech of the mind and of the heart, lodged within it, of which he speaks at such length in the preface of the Scholia to the Questions to Thalassius, is rather the parent of action and holds whatever of goodness is in it. On this matter see Gregory's oration on the great Athanasius.

text: Τῆς μὲν ὀδύνης, ἡ ἡδονή. Sunt quidem hæc, alia aliis causa, uti aliis locis ipse Maximus explicat; dumque sectamur voluptatem, nos laboribus implicamus, ac dolorem augemus, ipsumque jugem reddimus. Hic tamen, et quod attinet ad rationem Maximo allatam, potius scribendum videatur, τῆς μὲν ἡδονῆς, ἡ ὀδύνη· Dolor causa est voluptatis; quod ejus depellendi causa, voluptatem consectamur. Pleniora forte scripsit Maximus : quanquam pronum est permutatas has voces ex litterarum vicinitate.
anchorLine: νης, ἡ ἡδονή (b)· θέλοντες γὰρ ἐκφυγεῖν τὴν κατὰ
en: "Of pain, pleasure." These things are so indeed, one being the cause of another, as Maximus himself explains elsewhere; and while we pursue pleasure we entangle ourselves in toils, increase pain, and make it lasting. Yet here, in view of the reasoning Maximus gives, one should rather write "of pleasure, pain": pain is the cause of pleasure, since we pursue pleasure in order to drive pain away. Perhaps Maximus wrote it more fully; although it is easy to see these words exchanged because of the likeness of their letters.

text: Καὶ οὐκ ἐπιμελῶς. Allusio est ad Gen. vi, 5. ubi sic ἐπιμελῶς, quasi serio, omnique diligentia atque opera dicuntur, illius ætatis homines malo incumbere : quod procul est ab eo, qui illud odit, peneque invitus vel concupiscentia, vel suasione aliqua aut etiam errore, in illud quandoque trahitur.
anchorLine: ιβʹ. Ὀλιγάκις μὲν καὶ οὐκ ἐπιμελῶς (c) εὑρίσκε-
en: "And not carefully." An allusion to Gen. vi, 5, where "carefully" is used, as it were in earnest and with every diligence and effort, of the men of that age applying themselves to evil. That is far from the man who hates it and is drawn into it, almost unwillingly, now and then by desire, or by some persuasion, or even by error.

text: Κατὰ τὴν ἔλλειψιν τῆς ἐμπράκτου ζωῆς. Videtur τὴν ἔμπρακτον ζωήν, quasi activam dicere, seu, quæ actionem colit, et contra Θεωρητικὴν dividitur : velitque plures non admodum exercitatos in vita activa et actionis cultu, quasi per rationes superiores vi contemplationis Deoque illustrante prudentiæ munere nactos esse. Anceps usus τοῦ, κατὰ, dubium sensum reddit. Verius hic Maximus dixerit, quam in cap. De cha[...]itate ad Elpidium, esse aliqua difficilia, et quæ semel et iterum legi oporteat, ut percipiantur, nec solum ex phrasi et usu loquendi, sed magis ex ipsa materia, ipsa ex reconditiore penu moralis et Christianæ philosophiæ petita.
anchorLine: ἐμπράκτου ζωῆς (d), καὶ τὸ φρονεῖν ἐκληρώσαντο.
en: "By the lack of the active life." He seems to mean by "the active life" (so to speak the practical life), the one that cultivates action and is divided off against the contemplative; and he wishes that many, not greatly practised in the active life and the cultivation of action, had obtained the gift of prudence as it were through higher reasons, by the power of contemplation and with God shedding light. The ambiguous use of "κατά" leaves the sense doubtful. Maximus might more truly say here, as in the chapter On Charity to Elpidius, that there are some difficult matters which must be read once and again to be understood, not only from the phrasing and the way of speaking, but still more from the subject matter itself, drawn from the deeper store of moral and Christian philosophy.

text: Ἐν τῷ τῆς ἀναλγησίας νοσοκομείῳ. Ἀναλγησία hic Maximo, palam stupor mentis, quo quis cœlestium, et eorum quæ sunt ad salutem, omni sensu careat; vixque ac ne vix quidem meliori fruge renovari valeat. Jungit Marcus semel et iterum, De just. et operibus, c. 122 et 133, τὸ, ἡδυπαθὴς et ἀνάλγητος, qui sit voluptarius, sicque corporis deliciis deditus, ut illis sensum omnem pietatis exuerit; nedum erga proximos, per immisericordiam, uti expressit Obsop., sed magis erga Deum propriamque salutem.
anchorLine: μείῳ (e) μὴ αἰσχυνόμενος.
en: "In the hospital of insensibility." Insensibility (analgesia) here in Maximus is plainly a stupor of mind by which a man lacks all sense of heavenly things and of what pertains to salvation, and can hardly, or not even hardly, be renewed to better fruit. Mark (the Hermit) joins together, again and again, in On Those Justified by Works, chapters 122 and 133, the words "given to pleasure" and "insensible": one who is a voluptuary and so given over to bodily delights that he has lost all sense of piety; much less toward neighbours, through lack of compassion, as Obsopoeus rendered it, but still more toward God and his own salvation.

text: Ὁ τῷ λυπήσαντι ἀδίκως. Coactus sum mutare quod mendosum omnino apparebat, nulloque apto sensu a Maximo scribi poterat, λυπήσαντι δικαίως, et μετανοῶν· cum alioqui expedita sit totius capitis sententia, ipsa arguta, ac qua erudite exponuntur gradus ferendi aut remittendi injurias; quæ tunc injuriæ sunt, cum injuste inferuntur : ἀντὶ τοῦ μετανοῶν, scripsissem μετευνοῶν, si illa voce usum aliquem probatum auctorem invenissem. Alioqui vero vox εὐνοῶν, ipsa non incommoda; respexeritque in ea Maximus, illud Matth. v, 25 : Ἴσθι εὐνοῶν τῷ ἀντιδίκῳ σου ταχύ· Habeto benevolentiam cum adversario tuo cito, uti reddit Erasm. ac Græca sonant; spectatque et istud ad reconciliationem, qua studemus, injuriæ obliti, si quid ea læsa benevolentia est, saniori consilio resarcire.
anchorLine: λε΄. Ὁ τῷ λυπήσαντι ἀδίκως (f) πρὸ τοῦ προσ-
en: "He who has grieved (another) unjustly." I was compelled to alter what appeared wholly faulty and could not have been written by Maximus with any fitting sense, reading "having grieved justly, and repenting"; although otherwise the sense of the whole chapter is straightforward, pointed, and sets out learnedly the degrees of bearing or remitting injuries, which are injuries when they are inflicted unjustly. Instead of "repenting" I would have written "being well-disposed (metheunoon)", if I had found an approved author using that word. As it is, the word "eunoon" (well-disposed) is not unfitting, and Maximus may have had in view that saying in Matt. v, 25: "Be well-disposed toward your adversary quickly" ("Habeto benevolentiam cum adversario tuo cito", as Erasmus renders it, and as the Greek sounds); and this too looks to the reconciliation we seek, forgetting injuries, if anything of benevolence has been hurt, to repair it by a sounder counsel.

text: Παραμετρεῖσθαι τοῖς ἐλαχίστοις. Hæc humilitatis perfectio est, ac quod Dominus aliis verbis admonuit, jubens sedere in novissimo loco; ut nemo sit inter minimos, cujus nos modum excedere existimemus. Secus de superbis 37, nec æqualibus ait (τοῖς ἰσοτίμοις) in bonis velle παραμετρεῖσθαι, componi et exæquari.
anchorLine: χωρίς, ὃς οὐδὲ παραμετρεῖσθαι τοῖς ἐλαχίστοις (g)
en: "To be measured alongside the least." This is the perfection of humility, and what the Lord admonished in other words, bidding us sit in the lowest place, so that there be no one among the least whose measure we think we exceed. It is otherwise with the proud (chapter 37): he says they are unwilling, in good things, to be measured alongside, set level with, and made equal to their equals (tois isotimois).

text: LXX in eo Eccles. loco, non admodum probatis Græcis auctoribus trita. Affine tamen est, quod in plurium majore Lexico, alias Crispiniano refertur ex Plutar. in Romulo, Τούτους ἐξέκρουε καὶ παρῆγεν ὁ Τάτιος. Quasi expunxit ac missos fecit : quod et vox Hebraica sonat ותעבר transire fecit. Apud Paulum, τὸ, Παράγει γὰρ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου, I Cor. vii, 31, quod vulg. Præterit figura mundi hujus; perinde reddi posset : Fallax est species mundi hujus, quod scilicet mortalium oculis in rebus humanis objicit, a quibus Paulus discipulorum avocat animos, ne se illis dementari sinant, ipsis adhærendo, sed magis ad ea quæ vere sunt studium omne transferant, levi solum rerum usu permisso ac qualem vitæ necessitas alio festinantibus omnino postulat. Pro ἐπιθυμίας Vulg, malitia, ex Heb. cujus vocis explicatio est, τὸ, ἐπιθυμία· hæc enim carnis malitia seu vitium, concupiscentia.
anchorNote: continuation of note (i) begun on p-0719; call (i) stands on p-0719 after καρδίας
en: [the Seventy] in that passage of Ecclesiastes, a sense not much attested among Greek authors. Yet it is akin to what is cited in the larger Lexicon of several authors (otherwise Crispin's), from Plutarch in the Life of Romulus: "Tatius was expelling these and sending them away", that is, he struck them out and dismissed them; which the Hebrew word also means, "he caused to pass over". In Paul, the phrase "for the fashion of this world passes away" (I Cor. vii, 31), which the Vulgate renders "the figure of this world passes", could equally be rendered "deceptive is the appearance of this world", because it presents itself to mortal eyes in human affairs; Paul calls his disciples' minds away from these, so that they do not let themselves be fooled by them by clinging to them, but carry all their zeal over to what truly is, the use of things being permitted only lightly and only so far as the necessity of life demands for those hastening elsewhere. For the Vulgate's "malitia" in place of "epithymias" (desire), from the Hebrew: the explanation of that word is "epithymia"; for this is the malice or vice of the flesh, concupiscence.

text: Ἔτι δὲ παραμένει τοῦ φάρυγγος. Nempe diuturniora gulæ prælia, nec nisi morte finienda; quod absolvi a necessario ciborum usu, quandiu vita superstes est, minime liceat; cui conjuncta illa gulæ voluptas, ipsa necessaria Deoque auctore insita, quandiu justæ mediocritatis modum servat. Secus de venereorum voluptate, ordinata ad speciei conservationem, cujus rei munus, nec ad omnes, nec pro omni statu aut ætate spectat. Erat mendose, παρειμένου τοῦ φάρυγγος· quæ sic aperta imperiti scribæ menda, nolim excoquere, aut possim, indeque lectori negotium facessere.
anchorLine: παραμένει τοῦ φάρυγγος (j), τῷ μὴ φθάσαντι ταύ-
en: "And the throat remains." That is, the battles of the gullet are the longer-lasting and can be ended only by death; for release from the necessary use of food is by no means allowed while life remains, and joined to it is the gullet's pleasure, itself necessary and planted by God, so long as it keeps the measure of due moderation. It is otherwise with the pleasure of sexual things, which is ordered to the preservation of the species, a function that does not concern all persons, nor every state or age. The text read in error "the throat having been relaxed" (pareimenou tou pharyngos); an error so evident, that of an unskilled scribe, I would not care to gloss over, nor could I, and so give the reader trouble.

text: Ἐμπάθεια. Carnalis affectus, maxime venereorum, qui Maximo passim, ἐμπαθὴς λογισμός, ac jactu maxime consummatur; vere κατ' ἐξοχὴν πάθος, ob tactus majorem delectationem. ἡδυπάθεια, in aliis sensibus captata voluptas et jucunditas : προσπάθεια, mentis ipsa affectio, quæ se proclive abduci sinat. Sed hæc satis arbitraria, ut quæ sequentibus in his vocibus Græca facilitate Maximus ludit; quarum lepos atque vis, nullis satis Latinis vocibus potest repræsentari.
anchorLine: ο΄. Ὕλη πονηρὰ, σώματος μὲν ἐμπάθεια (k), ψυχῆς
en: "Empatheia." Carnal affection, above all of sexual things, which in Maximus is everywhere the "passionate thought"; and it is brought to completion above all by touch [printed 'jactu', the first letter damaged]; truly the passion par excellence, because of the greater delight of touch. Hedypatheia is pleasure and enjoyment taken in the other senses; prospatheia is the very inclination of the mind, which lets itself be readily led away. But these are rather arbitrary, as Maximus plays in the following chapters with these words in Greek with ease; their charm and force cannot be rendered by any Latin words.

text: Νεκροὶ ἐκ ζώντων. Paul. Rom. vi, 13, ἐκ νεκρῶν ζῶντας dixit, ex mortuis viventes; quæ verba sic videtur Maximus detorsisse, ut quod ille de animi morte vitaque dixerat, ipse ad corporis traheret : quæ quidem futura sit omnium at non laudabilis mors animi, quam νεκρώσεως vocabulo passim viri ecclesiastici Paulina phrasi vocant.
anchorLine: ος΄. Νεκροὶ μὲν ἐκ ζώντων (l) πάντες ὀφθήσον-
en: "Dead from living." Paul, Rom. vi, 13, said "living from the dead" (ex mortuis viventes); Maximus seems to have twisted these words so as to carry over to the body what Paul had said of the death and life of the soul: it is the death of all, but not a praiseworthy death, a death of the soul, which churchmen everywhere call by the word "nekrosis", in Paul's manner of speaking.

text: Πρὸς τὴν τῶν κατασκόπων ἀπαντήσεται πόλιν. Ad Sionem scilicet, cujus nomen speculam sonat, ac cujus ipsius Isaias meminit cap. illo LI, quo ista omnia Maximi collineant, consueta illi allegoria; quanquam hic eis longe solito parcior est, ut et capitibus de charitate.
anchorLine: πρὸς τὴν τῶν κατασκόπων ἀπαντήσεται πόλιν (m),
en: "He will come upon the city of the watchmen." That is, to Sion, whose name means a watchtower, and which Isaiah himself mentions in that chapter li, to which all these sayings of Maximus point, by the allegory customary to him; although here he is far more sparing of it than usual, as also in the chapters on charity.

text: Ὑπομένειν ἡμᾶς τῇ πίστει. Sic legisse Maximum Rom. xii, 12, ubi nunc Græca, τῇ θλίψει, Vulg. in tribulatione patientes; nihil dubium : utque alii codices suffragarentur, illa lectio magis arrideret, quod præsertim constructio ipsa mollior; quodque adeo duplicem virtutem Paulus continua serie videtur commendare, ac cuique quod illi proprium aut conjunctum est, tribuere : spei, gaudium, τῇ ἐλπίδι χαίροντες· fidei, laborum sustinentiam, τῇ πίστει ὑπομένοντες· quod ipsum argumentum late prosequitur in Epist. ad Hebr., ostendens omni retro ævo sanctos illa victores laborum exstitisse : cum illud, τῇ θλίψει ὑπομένοντες, duram omnino constructionem habeat, et in qua aliquid desideretur, necessario supplendum; nec satis antecedentibus aut sequentibus cohæreat : tametsi habent etiam Chrys., Theodor., Theophyl., etc. Cumque superioribus illud hæserit, τῷ καιρῷ δουλεύοντες, quod repræsentant Græcæ omnes editiones (si forte Parisiensem τῶν LXX, seu illis adjunctam Novi Testam. ad exemplar Romanum expressam exceperis) Erasm. temporì servientes, sic abhorrente sententia, nec satis Paulo digna, pro eo quod legerunt antiqui omnes relati, et Vulg. habetque cod. Alexand. τῷ Κυρίῳ δουλεύοντες, Domino servientes; quid mirum potuisse, pro, τῇ πίστει, τῇ θλίψει, sic una serie textu ibi laborante obrepere? Maximo, ex meliori codice emendante; si tamen ille ex codice scripsit, non ut suggerebat memoria : quæ sæpius id repræsentat, non quod in codice legimus, sed quod κατὰ πρόχειρον accommodatius nobis videtur : quomodo etiam Hieronymo sæpius obrepsisse observat Joan. Morinus, in Exercit. biblicis; potiorique ratione aliis, quorum in divinis non tanta fuit ἀκρίβεια. Hincque est, ut nihil affirmare ausim, ac donec occurrant certiora monumenta, mutandum contendere. Satis fuit aliam ejus loci lectionem, quæ tanti videatur, Maximo auctore utcunque vindicare ac declarare.
anchorLine: πϛ΄. Ὑπομένειν μὲν ἡμᾶς τῇ πίστει (n) παρα-
en: "That we endure by faith." Maximus read thus at Rom. xii, 12, where the Greek now has "in tribulation" (te thlipsei), the Vulgate "patient in tribulation"; no doubt of it: and even if other codices supported it, that reading would please more, since above all the construction itself is smoother, and Paul seems to commend a double virtue in continuous sequence, assigning to each what is proper or joined to it: to hope, joy ("rejoicing in hope"); to faith, endurance of labours ("enduring by faith"). Paul pursues this very argument at length in the Epistle to the Hebrews, showing that in every past age the saints were victors over labours. Whereas "enduring in tribulation" has a wholly harsh construction, one in which something must be supplied, and it does not cohere well with what precedes and follows, although Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, etc. have it. And since "serving the time" (to kairo douleuontes) has clung to the preceding words, which all Greek editions present (unless you except, perhaps, the Paris edition of the Septuagint, or the New Testament appended to it and printed after the Roman exemplar), Erasmus's "temporì servientes" is so at odds with the sense, and scarcely worthy of Paul, whereas all the ancients reported, and the Vulgate, and the Alexandrian codex have "serving the Lord" (to Kyrio douleuontes): what wonder that in place of "by faith" and "in tribulation" such a reading should creep in in a single sequence where the text is troubled? Maximus, correcting from a better codex, if indeed he wrote from a codex and not as memory suggested, which often reproduces not what we read in the codex but what comes more readily to hand: as Jean Morin observes in his Biblical Exercitations that it often happened to Jerome too, and with more reason to others, whose accuracy in divine matters was not so great. So I would dare assert nothing, and contend for a change only when more certain evidence turns up. It was enough to defend and set out, on Maximus's authority, another reading of that place that seems worth the notice.

text: Ἐν οἷς χρονίζει. Sententia est, quam et videatur ab auctore superiori mutuatus; qua significatur placere quæ molita sunt exque consuetudine, vel si alias injucunda sint. Describit Marc. De justitia ex oper. c. 68, durum mentis certamen, cum ab occupata olim informatione, ἀπὸ χρονίας προλήψεως; avellendus est animus, quasi tortoribus hinc inde cor distrahentibus : ubi frigide Obsop. temporali occupatione.
anchorLine: εχεῖ· καὶ γὰρ ἐν οἷς, φησὶ, χρονίζει (o), ἐν αὐτοῖς
en: "In which he lingers." The thought is one he seems to have borrowed from an earlier author; it signifies that things done, and from custom, please, even if they are otherwise unpleasant. Mark (the Hermit), On Those Justified by Works, ch. 68, describes the hard struggle of the mind when it must be torn away from a long-held preoccupation (apo chronias propleipseos), as though torturers were pulling the heart apart on both sides; where Obsopoeus, flatly, has "temporali occupatione".

text: Εὐχὴ μονολόγιστος. Interpretatur Hesych. μονόκλονος, exque eo Varin. Quod sit obscurum per obscurius. Marc. De justitia ex operib. c. 140, μονολόγιστον ἐλπίδα habet, quam et parari δι᾿ ἀρνήσεως dicit. Ὅταν ὁ νοῦς κρατήσῃ δι᾿ ἀρνήσεως τὴν μονολόγιστον ἐλπίδα· ubi primum ex Maximo emend. δι᾿ ἀπαρνήσεως· non enim vox illa simplex eo sensu usurpatur : ἀπάρνησις vero, rerum abdicatio est, ipsaque nostris abnegatio qua sic spes μονολόγιστος obtinetur, ac μονολόγιστος ipsa gratia paratur : quam vocem Hesych. interpretatus sit ἀκλόντηπος [...] ut irrepserunt in ejus Lexicon plura menda. Quadrat enim optime, ut spes sic μονολόγιστος dicatur, quasi minime cogitationibus anceps, sed ipsa unius rationis et inturbata ; eodemque modo oratio. Non quod reddidit Obsop. Marci loco citato, spem unice considerandam. Iterum, c. 102, ὁ μονολόγιστον ἐξανύων εὐχήν, intra velamen versari Maximo dicitur, opponitque τῷ ἐν αὐτῇ ῥεμβομένῳ, qui vaga mente in ea sit, segniusque oret, nec sobria ac attenta mente. Nam et Chrysost. in Epist. ad Coloss. τῷ γρηγοροῦντι καὶ νήφοντι opponit : cui proinde idem est ac ἀκηδιῶν qui segnis tepidusque est : quo fere sensu etiam μετέωρον haud raro Patres dicunt : quod et Hesych. κοῦφον reddit et ἐνυπνιῶδες levem, stultum; suspensi scilicet vagique ac instabilis animi.
anchorLine: [Greek column, ch. on μονολόγιστος εὐχή; call (p) in the text]
en: "Prayer of a single thought (monologistos)." Hesychius explains it as "monoklonos", and Varinus after him: so the obscure is explained by the more obscure. Mark, On Those Justified by Works, ch. 140, has "monologiston hope", which he also says is obtained by renunciation. "When the mind prevails by denial the monologistos hope": where, the first time, it should be emended from Maximus to "by apoarnesis" (renunciation), for that word is not used in that sense in the simple form; apoarnesis is the giving up of things, and our own self-denial by which hope is thus made monologistos, and monologistos itself is obtained by grace; a word Hesychius explained as [...], as many faults have crept into his Lexicon. It fits very well that hope should be called monologistos, as being by no means divided in thoughts but of one undisturbed reasoning; and so with prayer. Not as Obsopoeus rendered it in Mark's passage, 'hope to be uniquely considered.' Again, ch. 102: the one who completes a monologistos prayer is said by Maximus to be within the veil, and he opposes him to the one tossed about (rhembomenos) in it, who with wandering mind is in it and prays rather listlessly, not with a sober and attentive mind. Chrysostom too, on Colossians, opposes it to the one who is watchful and sober, for whom, accordingly, it is the same as 'sluggish', i.e. one who is slack and lukewarm; in nearly which sense the Fathers also often say 'suspended' (meteoron), which Hesychius also renders 'light' and 'dreamy, light, foolish': that is, of a suspended, wandering and unstable mind.

text: Ἐν δὲ τῇ αἰσθήσει γενόμενος. Sunt hæc quasi ænigmatica. Quid sit mentem esse in sensu, dumque in illo est, et conceptus habere et ratio-cinationes ; id est, res simpliciter et cum discursu intelligere, haud satis capio, nisi hoc vult Maximus, intelligentem nunquam absolvi, pro hoc sta-
anchorLine: ἔστιν. Ἐν δὲ τῇ αἰσθήσει γενόμενος (q), μετὰ πάν-
en: "But having come to be in sense-perception." These things are, as it were, enigmatic. What it is for the mind to be in sense-perception, and while it is in it to have conceptions and reasonings, that is, to understand things simply and with discursive thought, I scarcely grasp, unless Maximus means this, that the one who understands is never released, for this ... [the note breaks off at the foot of the page and continues on p-0726].

text: tu, a phantasmate, quod sensui ascribit. Sive enim ipsam rei quidditatem intelligat, quod vocat νόημα (id est conceptum mentis ac intellectum), sive circa accidentia et proprietates discurrat, quod λογισμὸν indigetat, omnino necesse est, ut phantasma, quasi omnis ejus cognitionis basim, speculetur, in quo et accidentia, et ipsa essentia illis involuta, eluceat. Τὰ λογικὰ quod vocat, ea quæ discursu ac ratione cogitante intelliguntur (passive scilicet utendo illa voce) paulo insolentius est. Affine tamen est, quod λογικὴν στάσιν dicunt rhetores, statum rationalem. Quintilianus, l. iii, c. 5 : Illud jam omnes fatentur, esse quæstiones aut in scripto, aut in non scripto : in scripto, sunt de jure : in non scripto, de re : illud legale, hoc rationale. Hermagoras atque eum secuti vocant, νομικὸν et λογικόν. Item Cicero, Tusc. l. iv : Habes ea quæ de perturbationibus enucleatius disputant Stoici : quæ λογικὰ appellant, quia asseruntur subtilius. Sic itaque hic Maximus, λογικά, non ipsa ratione prædita, sed quæ sic ratione percipiuntur ; et quæ rationalia, eadem cum Græcis vocis ὁμωνυμίᾳ cogimur dicere, quod non distinctæ voces, ut sunt τὸ νοητὸν et τὸ νοερὸν etsi nec in illis auctores satis accurati sunt, nec, raro eorum significata confundant, ac quod passive sonat, active accipiant, vicissimque.
anchorNote: continuation of note (q) begun on p-0725; call (q) stands on p-0725 after γενόμενος
en: [...] by the act, by the imagination, which he ascribes to sense-perception. For whether the mind understands the very essence of a thing, which he calls noema (that is, a concept or understanding of the mind), or ranges over accidents and properties, which needs reasoning (logismos), it is altogether necessary that it contemplate the phantasm, as the basis of all its knowledge, in which both the accidents and the essence itself, wrapped up in them, shine forth. His "ta logika", meaning things understood by discursive reasoning (the word being used passively), is a little unusual. It is akin, however, to what the rhetoricians call the "logical status", the rational issue. Quintilian, III, 5: "All admit that questions are either in what is written or in what is not written: in what is written, they concern law; in what is not written, the matter: the former legal, the latter rational." Hermagoras and his followers call them nomikon and logikon. Likewise Cicero, Tusc. IV: "You have what the Stoics argue more minutely about the passions: which they call logika, because they are asserted more subtly." So here Maximus's logika are not things endowed with reason but things perceived by reason; and what are rational (rationalia) we are forced to call by the same word, by the Greeks' homonymy, because the words are not distinct, as are to noeton and to noeron, although the authors are not careful enough even there, and often confuse their meanings and take actively what sounds passive, and the reverse.

text: Λιπαρῶν τὸν μέτοχον. Placebat magis ut esset τὸν κάτοχον. Rogans eum, qui vir spiritalis sit, ἔνθεος, plenus Spiritu ac oratione provectus, ejusque nactus perfectionem ; quique adeo quiete in illa fruatur ; præ laboris scilicet impatientia, ut in aliis sic dissipatis (actioni scilicet addictum) morari sinat : ac vel maxime, quod ea vox κάτοχο, etiam activam significationem quandoque admittat. Sic enim ille in orationis exercitio detinentem Patrem spiritalem, ab ea dimittere, sic quasi tædio victus propense roget.
anchorLine: ρων τὸν μέτοχον (r) ἀπολυθῆναι, πρὸς τὰ ἀφ᾿ ὧν
en: "Pressing the partner." I should have preferred 'ton katochon' (the one possessed/holding). He asks the man who is spiritual, inspired (entheos), full of the Spirit and advanced in prayer, who has attained its perfection and so enjoys it in quiet, to permit himself, through impatience of labour, to linger among other distracted people (one given to action), and above all because that word katocho sometimes admits an active meaning too. So he thus asks, as if overcome by weariness, that the spiritual Father who holds him in the exercise of prayer let him go from it.

text: Τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ ὁ δημαγωγός. Josue scilicet, qui sic duos viros, sive ut habent οἱ LXX, νεανίσκους, juvenes, exploratum misit, omni jam deserti superato itinere. Exponit autem Maximus allegorice, τὴν ὀπτικὴν καὶ ἐποπτικὴν αὐτοῦ δύναμιν· cernendi vim et inspiciendi, sensum scilicet et intellectum ; id est mentem, quæ est vis illa ἐποπτική, qua licet tantisper ipsa divina inspicere, et παρακύπτειν, quasi a longe avide inclinando prospicere : quæ vitæ hujus summa nostra perfectio est. De Mose, qui velit accipere, qui et ipse speculatores misit, et a longe etiam terram aspexit, monstrante illi Deo e monte, cum moriturus esset, nec hic a Maximi scopo abierit: nam et hanc ἐποπτείαν sit et quanta mortalibus concessa Dei notitia ac speraæ beatitudinis.
anchorLine: ὁ δημαγωγός (s) κατασκοπεῖν δύναται τὴν γῆν τῆς
en: "The leader of Israel." That is, Joshua, who thus sent out two men, or, as the Seventy have it, young men (neaniskous), to spy out the land, when the whole journey of the desert had been completed. Maximus explains allegorically "his power of sight and of overlooking": the power of discerning and inspecting, that is of sense and of intellect; that is, the mind, which is that power of epopteia by which it may for a time itself behold divine things and peep out (parakyptein), as if leaning eagerly from afar to look out: which is the sum of our perfection in this life. [The note then turns to Moses, who also sent spies and himself saw the land from afar, God showing it to him from the mountain when he was about to die, and says that this too is not away from Maximus's purpose.]

text: Ἐν καινότητι ζωῆς πολιτεύσασθαι. Posuerit Maximus hanc vocem, ut exponentem eam, qua Paulus usus est, περιπατήσωμεν, quam et expressi in versione. Sic enim ambulare, conversari est, talibusque rationibus ac disciplina vitam componere et exigere. Legisse Maximum πολιτευσώμεν, non ausim asserere.
anchorLine: τῷ ὁ τοιοῦτος, ἐν καινότητι ζωῆς πολιτεύσασθαι (u).
en: "To live as a citizen in newness of life." Maximus may have set down this word as explaining the one Paul used, "let us walk" (peripatesomen), which I also expressed in my version. For to walk thus is to conduct oneself, and to arrange and carry on one's life by such principles and discipline. That Maximus read "politeusomen" I would not dare to assert.

text: Περιεκτικωτέρων ἀρετῶν. Sic et Marcus generales virtutes vocat : præcepta quoque generalia et particularia, cap. 25 De justitia ex oper. ἐντολὴν περιεκτικὴν dicit, qua Deus jubet πᾶσιν ἀποτάξασθαι τοῖς ὑπάρχουσιν· abrenuntiare omnibus facultatibus : μερικὴν, qua μεταδοῦναι τῷ μὴ ἔχοντι, tribuere ei qui non habet. De oratione, cap. 89, πᾶσαν ἐργασίαν ἐντολῶν ἐν αὐτῇ περιεχλεῖσθαι· included in ea omnem operationem virtutum : quam et κεφαλαιωδεστέραν maxime probat, cap. 154, sic nimirum summariam, ut nihil in specie oremus, sed solum Dei regnum et doctrinam ejus quæramus. Hic Maximus generales virtutes vocat, quæ pluribus, seu etiam omnibus conducant ; non quod alias omnes complectantur ; qua ratione sola dilectio Dei et proximi, omnium ἐντολῶν περιεκτικωτάτη merito Marco dicitur, cap. 211, δευτέρα κεχαρισμένη τροφή, cibus sit in secundis concessus ; nempe corporalis, pro justa corporis necessitate, ejusque indulgentia, Dei munere donatus.
anchorLine: ἀρετῶν (v), νηστείας, εὐχῆς τε καὶ σιωπῆς, ἀναγ-
en: "Of the more comprehensive virtues." Mark (the Hermit) likewise calls them general virtues: he also speaks of general and particular precepts, in chapter 25 of On Those Justified by Works, a "comprehensive commandment" by which God bids us renounce all our possessions (abrenuntiare omnibus facultatibus), and a "partial" one, by which we are to give to the one who has not. In On Prayer, ch. 89, he says that every work of the commandments is enclosed in it, and he especially approves it as more summary in chapter 154, so summary that we pray for nothing in particular but seek only God's kingdom and his teaching. Here Maximus calls those virtues general which serve many, or even all; not because they embrace all the others, in which sense only the love of God and neighbour is rightly called by Mark the most comprehensive of all commandments. In chapter 211 Mark says "a second, graciously given food": food granted in the second things, that is bodily food, for the just need of the body and its indulgence, given by God's gift.
continuedColumn: note runs from the left half to the right half of the page

text: Εὐχερῶς καὶ μὴ προσηκόντως. Addidi negationem, quod vocum opposita omnino ratio, nec possit aliquis sic εὐχερῶς, levi ex causa et temere ad sensilia descendere, et προσηκόντως, convenienter justaque et æqua ratione ; quomodo etiam perfecti in illis versantur, nullo aut levi suo detrimento, quod ipsum luculenter justæ necessitatis sarciat ratio, ac charitatis ipsa lex : nec Maximus ab ejusmodi descensu, sua hac sententia ac exemplo, debuit deterrere, sed solum a priore. Quod erat ἐν τοῖς θείοις, mutavi ἐν τοῖς οἰκείοις. Plane enim componit mentem secum ipsam, ut spiritalia sectatur, et ut se ad sensum demittit : quo priore modo in propriis versatur, et ut mens agit, τὸ, ἐν τῷ μάχεσθαι, proclive mutem, πρὸ τοῦ μάχεσθαι· ante pugnam, quæ certe magna ducis imprudentia est, dum copias deterit quasi velitando et excurrendo, ante justi prælii molem, quo de rerum summa decernendum sit.
anchorLine: εὐχερῶς καὶ [μὴ] προσηκόντως (x) κατέρχεται, πει-
en: "Easily and not fittingly." I have added the negation, because the opposite of the words is wholly the reasoning, and no one could descend to sensible things 'easily' (on a slight and rash cause) and 'fittingly' (suitably, and by just and equitable reason); just as the perfect also dwell among them with no or slight harm to themselves, which the reason of just necessity and the law of charity itself amply makes good. And Maximus, by this sentence and example, ought not to have deterred from such a descent, but only from the former. What was 'in divine things' I have changed to 'in one's own things'. For he plainly sets the mind in order with itself, as it pursues spiritual things and as it lets itself down to sense; in the former way it dwells in its own things, and as the mind acts, I would readily change 'in fighting' (en to machesthai) to 'before fighting' (pro tou machesthai): before battle, which is certainly a great imprudence in a general, while he wears out his forces by skirmishing and sallying before the weight of a just battle by which the sum of things is to be decided.

text: Νόες μόνοι γυμνοὶ σωμάτων. Quas hic mentes vocat Maximus, ipsæ sint quæ cogitationes succendunt atque dæmones, sic nimirum profligatæ vitæ hominibus præsentiam aut quasi præsentiam, nudam exhibentes : velut etiam mentes sanctæ, eximiæ sanctitatis viris, quandoque ipsæ, non in somnis, aut moventes vim cogitandi; sed coram præsentia quasi corporali apparent, divinaque eos docent : qui gradus prophetiæ aliis jam dictis, auctore etiam angelico Doctore, altior exsistit. Obscura tamen tota hic Maximi mens et doctrina, ac num ipsi sine discursu conceptus mentis altiores, ita, vocati νόες.
anchorLine: μόνοι γυμνοὶ σωμάτων (y) αὐτῇ προσπελάζοντες,
en: "Minds alone, naked of bodies." The minds which Maximus here names are the very ones that kindle the thoughts and are the demons, thus presenting to men of a profligate life a naked presence or quasi-presence; as also holy minds sometimes appear to men of outstanding holiness, not in sleep, nor setting in motion the power of thinking, but before them as in a quasi-bodily presence, and teach them divine things: which degree of prophecy, as the Angelic Doctor too says of others already mentioned, stands higher. Yet the whole mind and teaching of Maximus here is obscure, and whether the concepts of the mind itself, without discursive reasoning, are higher ones, thus called noes.
continuedColumn: note runs from the left half to the right half of the page

text: Τὸν τῆς κενοδοξίας λογισμόν. Vitium sonat illa vox, cum de talibus dicitur. Vitiosas alii cogitationes, vocant, de quibus exstant Cassiani, Nili, et aliorum tractatus. Septem ergo seu vitiis, seu vitiosis cogitationibus, ipsaque postremo excussa inanis gloriæ labes, superest, ut octavam cogitationem, non jam vitiosam, sed quæ vitiis seu affectibus eliminatis succedit, superinduamus; quam communius Maximus aliique spirituales τὴν ἀπάθειαν vocant ; domicilium cœleste, quod gemitibus ac lacrymis paratur.
anchorLine: ρλδʹ. Ἕβδομον τὸν τῆς κενοδοξίας λογισμὸν (z)
en: "The thought of vainglory." That word means a vice when it is said of such things. Others call them vicious thoughts, on which there are treatises by Cassian, Nilus and others. When, then, the seven vices or vicious thoughts have been dealt with, and last of all the stain of vainglory shaken out, it remains that we put on over them an eighth thought, no longer vicious, but one that succeeds once vices or passions have been removed, which Maximus and other spiritual writers more commonly call apatheia (freedom from passion): a heavenly dwelling, prepared by groanings and tears.
